title: File-Based Routing
summary: In the Next.js App Router, **the file system is the router**: each folder under `app/` is a **route segment** and a `page.tsx` inside it makes that segment a navigable URL. **Special files** (`layout`, `page`, `loading`, `error`, `not-found`) add shared UI and states per segment, nested folders create **nested routes**, and you can **colocate** components, tests, and styles next to the route without them becoming pages.

subtopics.title: Folders are routes
subtopics.explanation: Under app/, every folder defines a route segment whose name becomes a URL path part. The folder alone is just a segment — it only becomes a navigable page when it contains a page file. This convention means your URL structure mirrors your folder tree, with no route table to maintain.

subtopics.title: page.tsx makes a route public
subtopics.explanation: A page.tsx (or page.jsx/.js) file inside a folder is what makes that route segment publicly accessible at its URL. Without a page file, the folder is just an organizational segment that can hold layouts or shared code but is not itself routable. The default export of page.tsx is the UI for that route.

subtopics.title: Nested routes
subtopics.explanation: Nesting folders creates nested URL paths. app/blog/page.tsx serves /blog and app/blog/[slug]/page.tsx serves /blog/:slug. Each level can also have its own layout, loading, and error files, which compose from the root down — so deeper routes inherit the UI shells of their ancestors.

subtopics.title: Special files: layout, page, loading, error, not-found
subtopics.explanation: Next.js reserves specific filenames per segment: layout.tsx wraps the segment and its children (and persists across navigation), page.tsx is the route UI, loading.tsx is a Suspense fallback shown while the segment loads, error.tsx (a Client Component) catches errors in the segment, and not-found.tsx renders for missing resources. Each is optional and applies to its segment subtree.
subtopics.example:
app/dashboard/
  layout.tsx    // shared shell
  page.tsx      // /dashboard
  loading.tsx   // loading UI
  error.tsx     // error boundary

subtopics.title: Route segments and the URL
subtopics.explanation: Each folder is a 'segment' of the path. Static segments map literally (settings -> /settings); dynamic segments use brackets ([id] -> /:id) to capture values; and route groups in parentheses ((marketing)) organize folders WITHOUT adding to the URL. Understanding segments explains exactly how a file path becomes a URL.

subtopics.title: Colocation
subtopics.explanation: You can place components, hooks, tests, and styles inside route folders and they will NOT become routes — only the reserved special files are treated as routing files. This lets you keep a route's private building blocks next to it (colocation) instead of in a distant shared folder, improving organization.
subtopics.example:
app/dashboard/
  page.tsx            // a route
  Chart.tsx           // NOT a route — colocated component
  utils.ts            // NOT a route — colocated helper

foundations.overview: File-based routing is the Next.js convention where the structure of the app/ directory defines the application's routes. Folders are route segments, a page.tsx makes a segment navigable, nesting creates nested URLs, and a small set of special files (layout, page, loading, error, not-found) attach shared UI and states to each segment. Non-special files colocated in a folder are ignored by the router.
foundations.formalDefinition: In the App Router, each directory under app/ is a route segment whose name contributes to the URL path. A reserved page file renders the segment's route; reserved layout/loading/error/not-found files provide composed UI and states. Dynamic segments use bracket syntax and route groups use parentheses, which organize without affecting the URL.
foundations.whyItMatters: File-based routing removes the boilerplate and drift of a manually maintained route table: the URL structure is always visible in the file tree, and shared UI/loading/error states attach by convention. It is the first thing you must understand to build anything in Next.js.
foundations.mentalModel: Picture the URL as a path you walk through folders: each folder you enter is a segment of the URL, the page.tsx in the final folder is what renders, and any layout.tsx files along the way wrap the result like nested frames.
foundations.browserPerspective: When a user navigates, Next.js resolves the URL to the matching folder, composes the layouts from the root down, and renders the leaf page. Shared layouts persist across navigations, so the browser only swaps the changing segment rather than reloading the whole shell.
foundations.realWorldUsage: Marketing sites use route groups to organize sections, blogs use dynamic [slug] segments, dashboards use nested layouts for persistent sidebars, and every app uses page.tsx files to expose its routes — all driven by folder structure.
foundations.businessImpact: Predictable, convention-based routing speeds up development and onboarding because the URL map is self-documenting, reducing time spent wiring and debugging routing configuration.
foundations.engineeringImpact: Engineers reason about routes by browsing folders, colocate route-specific code naturally, and get loading/error states by convention — but they must learn which filenames are reserved and how segments compose.
foundations.performanceImpact: Per-segment code splitting means each route loads only its own JS, and loading.tsx enables streaming so users see content sooner. Layouts persist across navigation, avoiding redundant re-rendering of shared shells.
commonUseCases: Exposing pages by adding page.tsx to a folder (e.g. app/pricing/page.tsx -> /pricing)
Nested layouts for persistent navigation in dashboards
Route groups (parentheses) to organize sections without changing URLs
Colocating route-specific components and helpers inside the route folder

commonMisconceptions.myth: Every file in a route folder becomes a route.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Only reserved files (page, layout, loading, error, not-found, route) are routing files; other files are safely colocated and ignored by the router.

commonMisconceptions.myth: A folder by itself creates a visitable URL.
commonMisconceptions.reality: A folder is just a segment; it only becomes a navigable route when it contains a page.tsx.

debuggingLab.title: My new route returns 404
debuggingLab.symptom: You created app/contact/Contact.tsx with the component, but visiting /contact returns 404 — the route doesn't exist.
debuggingLab.errorAnalysis: A folder becomes a navigable route only when it contains a reserved page file. Contact.tsx is a regular (colocated) component, which the router ignores, so the /contact segment has no page and returns 404. The file must be named page.tsx.
commonMistakes: Naming the route file after the component (Contact.tsx) instead of the reserved page.tsx.
Assuming any component file in a folder creates a route — only reserved files do.
debuggingLab.fixChallenge: Rename the file to page.tsx (or import the component into a page.tsx) so the segment becomes routable.

theory.question: How does file-based routing work in the Next.js App Router?
theory.directAnswer: In the App Router, the app/ directory's structure defines the routes: each folder is a route segment whose name becomes part of the URL, and a page.tsx inside a folder makes that segment a navigable route. Nesting folders creates nested URLs, dynamic segments use [brackets], and route groups use (parentheses) to organize without affecting the URL. Special files — layout, page, loading, error, not-found — attach shared UI and states to each segment, and non-reserved files are simply colocated and ignored by the router.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A convention where the file system is the route definition: folders are segments and page.tsx files are routes.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: To eliminate a manually maintained route table and make the URL map visible and self-documenting in the file tree.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Next.js resolves a URL by matching folders to segments, composing layouts from the root down, and rendering the leaf page.tsx.

theory.whyImportant: Routing is the first thing you touch in any Next.js app, and this convention underpins layouts, loading/error states, and code splitting — making it a standard beginner interview question.
theory.realWorldExample: app/blog/page.tsx serves /blog, app/blog/[slug]/page.tsx serves individual posts, and app/blog/layout.tsx provides a shared blog shell for both.

followUps.question: Why doesn't a folder alone create a route?
followUps.answer: A folder is just a segment; it needs a page.tsx to render UI and become navigable.

followUps.question: Do all files in app/ become routes?
followUps.answer: No — only reserved files (page, layout, loading, error, not-found, route) are routing files; others are colocated and ignored.

theory.question: What are the special files in an App Router segment and what does each do?
theory.directAnswer: Each route segment can include reserved files: layout.tsx wraps the segment and its children and persists across navigation; page.tsx is the route UI that makes the segment navigable; loading.tsx is a Suspense fallback shown while the segment loads; error.tsx is a Client Component error boundary for the segment; and not-found.tsx renders when a resource is missing or notFound() is called. Route handlers use route.ts. These compose from the root segment down.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A fixed set of reserved filenames that attach UI and behavior to a route segment.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: To provide shared layouts, loading, and error handling by convention instead of manual wiring in every page.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Next.js automatically wraps a segment's page with its layout, Suspense (loading), and error boundary (error) as it composes the tree.

theory.whyImportant: These conventions are how you build layouts, streaming, and resilient UIs in Next.js; interviewers check that you know them and how they nest.
theory.realWorldExample: A dashboard segment uses layout.tsx for the sidebar, loading.tsx for a skeleton, and error.tsx so a failed widget shows a fallback instead of crashing the page.

nestedTopics.title: Composition
nestedTopics.explanation: Layouts, loading, and error files nest and compose from the root segment downward.

nestedTopics.title: error is client
nestedTopics.explanation: error.tsx must be a Client Component because it uses an error boundary and a reset handler.

followUps.question: Where does loading.tsx get its behavior?
followUps.answer: It works via React Suspense — Next.js wraps the segment's page in a Suspense boundary whose fallback is loading.tsx.

scenario.question: You need marketing pages and an authenticated app under one Next.js project, with different layouts but clean URLs like /about and /dashboard (no /marketing or /app prefix). How do you structure the folders?
scenario.directAnswer: I'd use route groups: app/(marketing)/ with its own layout.tsx for public pages like about/page.tsx, and app/(app)/ with a different layout.tsx for authenticated pages like dashboard/page.tsx. Because folder names in parentheses are stripped from the URL, the routes stay clean (/about, /dashboard) while each group gets its own layout. Shared components live colocated or in a shared folder that the router ignores.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: Using route groups to apply different layouts without polluting the URL.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Real apps need distinct layouts for sections but want clean, prefix-free URLs.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Parenthesized folders organize the tree and carry their own layout.tsx, yet contribute nothing to the URL path.

scenario.whyImportant: Organizing routes and layouts cleanly is a practical, frequently-tested design skill in Next.js apps.

nestedTopics.title: Per-group layouts
nestedTopics.explanation: Each route group can define its own layout.tsx for its pages.

nestedTopics.title: URL stays clean
nestedTopics.explanation: Group names in parentheses never appear in the URL.

followUps.question: Could you do this without route groups?
followUps.answer: You could use literal folders like /marketing, but then the prefix appears in the URL; route groups give the layout separation while keeping URLs clean.

coding.question: Lay out the files for a blog with a list page, individual posts, a shared layout, and a loading state.
coding.thoughtProcess: The list lives at /blog, so app/blog/page.tsx. Individual posts are dynamic, so app/blog/[slug]/page.tsx reading the slug param. A shared shell for both is app/blog/layout.tsx, and a loading fallback is app/blog/loading.tsx. The dynamic page receives params with the slug.
coding.lineByLine: layout.tsx wraps every blog route with a shared shell. loading.tsx is the Suspense fallback for blog routes. page.tsx is the /blog list. [slug]/page.tsx is the dynamic route; it reads params.slug to fetch and render one post. Together they show segments, special files, and dynamic routing.
coding.timeComplexity: N/A — routing structure, not an algorithm.

alternativeApproaches.title: Pre-generate post params
alternativeApproaches.explanation: Use generateStaticParams to statically build each post route at build time.

followUps.question: How would you add a 404 for a missing post?
followUps.answer: Call notFound() when the fetch returns nothing, and add app/blog/[slug]/not-found.tsx (or a segment not-found.tsx) to render the missing-post UI.

productionDeepDive.architecture: Model the app as a tree of route segments under app/: a root layout.tsx, route groups to separate concerns (marketing vs authenticated) without URL prefixes, dynamic [segments] for resource pages, and per-segment layout/loading/error files. Colocate route-specific components and helpers inside their segment to keep cohesion high.
productionDeepDive.performance: File-based routing gives automatic per-route code splitting, so each page ships only its JS. loading.tsx enables streaming for faster perceived load, and persistent layouts avoid re-rendering shared shells across navigations.
productionDeepDive.security: Keep server-only logic in Server Components and route.ts handlers within the segment; never expose secrets through colocated client components. Use route groups and layouts to enforce consistent auth shells around protected segments.
productionDeepDive.scaling: As an app grows, segment-based organization and colocation keep routing comprehensible. Route groups prevent deep prefix nesting in URLs, and dynamic segments with generateStaticParams let large content sets pre-render at build time.
productionDeepDive.maintainability: Because the URL map equals the folder tree, routing is self-documenting and easy to navigate. Standardize where colocated code lives and which special files each segment uses so reviewers can scan structure quickly.
productionDeepDive.observability: The build output lists every route discovered from the file system and marks it static or dynamic, making it easy to confirm that intended routes (and only those) exist. Monitor 404s to catch missing or misnamed page files.

caseStudies.problem: Many sections needing different layouts and thousands of dynamic content pages with clean URLs.
caseStudies.solution: Route groups for per-section layouts, dynamic [slug] segments with generateStaticParams, and colocated components per route.
caseStudies.tradeoffs: Must learn the reserved-file conventions and segment composition, in exchange for a self-documenting, scalable routing structure.
caseStudies.lessons: Lean on conventions: page.tsx for routes, groups for layout separation, and colocation to keep route code cohesive.

keyTakeaways: In the App Router the file system is the router: each folder under app/ is a route segment and the segment's name becomes part of the URL.
A folder only becomes a navigable route when it contains a page.tsx; nesting folders creates nested URLs.
Special files attach behavior per segment: layout (shared, persistent shell), page (route UI), loading (Suspense fallback), error (boundary), not-found (missing resource).
Dynamic segments use [brackets] to capture URL values, and route groups use (parentheses) to organize folders without affecting the URL.
Only reserved files are routing files — other components, helpers, and tests can be safely colocated inside a route folder.
